# Research notes: history-r2 (topic discovery)

Scope: niche "history", about 10 minutes, English, illustrated stills, general YouTube audience. No processed references.
Budget used: 7 searches, 6 fetches (5 pages read, 1 refused with HTTP 403).

## Leads in mind before searching (recorded so the trail shows what memory brought)
The 1858 Atlantic telegraph cable, the Vasa (1628), the longitude problem, Roman concrete, the Antikythera mechanism, railway time, the tulip-mania myth, and the Great Stink of 1858.
I treated these as leads like any other. The first three searches surveyed the scope and were not aimed at any of them.

## Searches, in order
1. Survey of consequential decisions (overlooked turning points). Popular listicles: the Dunkirk halt order, Washington before Trenton, Custer at Little Bighorn, the Milan declaration of 313, the Defenestration of Prague, penicillin.
   Dropped: the battle decisions are famous, and their weight is the fighting itself. The Milan declaration's subject is religious. The Defenestration summary garbled its facts (it put a French king in Prague). Penicillin is famous and medical.
2. Survey of hard practical problems solved before modern technology. Ann Blair's early-modern "information overload" (Harvard Gazette), the steelyard (practice without theory), and the Mary Rose's gunports.
   Kept as an unread lead: information overload is a strong, different value form (a problem and its solutions), but its payoff is abstract. I could not read it at comparable depth alongside three finalists, so I did not rule it out on evidence; it simply was not taken further.
   Dropped: the Mary Rose (hundreds drowned, a story told through its victims, and the same design-failure form as the Vasa); the steelyard (looked thin for ten minutes on what I saw).
3. Survey of new evidence that changed what historians believed (2025). A CNN roundup (S11): pathogens in Napoleon's soldiers, Endurance's structure, the Tumat puppies, the settlement of Malta, gladiator bite marks, the Song of Wade.
   Kept: Endurance.
   Dropped under the content rules: the Napoleon study (mass death from disease, told by the dying), the bite marks (a body and its wounds), and the Song of Wade (its source is a sermon, and its point is supernatural creatures).
   Dropped as off-niche or thin: the puppies (prehistoric biology) and Malta (thin for this niche).
4. Endurance: Tuhkuri 2025 in Polar Record, plus NPR, Aalto, Smithsonian and Gizmodo coverage.
5. The 1858 cable: Linda Hall (Ashworth), PBS, IEEE Spectrum (Marsh), the Science Museum's object record of the coil, and Hunt's Imperial Science.
6. Tulips: Goldgar in History Today, the IHR review, Smithsonian 2018, History.com.
7. Thomson's law of squares: the Royal Society archive record of his letter to Stokes (primary, not read), the Glasgow Kelvin exhibition, and Wikipedia.

## Reads
- S1, the Tuhkuri paper: open access, body read in full. This is T2's strongest source, and it names its own limits and the opposing view (Bound 2022).
- S2, Marsh in IEEE Spectrum: read in full. It reports de Cogan's 1985 reassessment, which is what made T1's verdict genuinely open.
- History Today (Goldgar): refused with 403, so nothing was read there (S6).
- S5, Price's IHR review of Goldgar: read in full. This was T3's strongest source available to me.
- S3, Ashworth at Linda Hall: read in full. It confirms T1's core independently of S2.
- S4, the Glasgow Kelvin exhibition: the cable section read. It gives the law of squares in the right direction, plus the contracts-before-advice detail.

## Why T1, and where it was close
I read three independent sources for T1, one for T2 (the full study) and one for T3 (a review; the historian's own article was blocked).
T2 lost on what its read source itself says: one study, by the author's own account a simple dimensional analysis, which a named researcher contradicts, and which leaves the motive unknown. It did not lose for being unread. It was close.
T3's loss is partly a reading gap, and I say so plainly in its entry: the book's case records might supply the scenes the review lacks.

## Where I was unsure, or what is still to verify before a script
- S2 words the law of squares as "inversely proportional to the square" of the length. I take it as a slip and use S4's direction. Thomson's primary record (S9) is unread.
- The 16 hours for the Queen's 98 words (C04) rests on S2 alone, and the opening hook depends on it. Corroborate it first.
- The failure date: S3 gives 2 September, S4 counts 23 days, S2 says "within a few weeks". The script says "within weeks".
- That Whitehouse secretly used Thomson's galvanometer (C11) rests on S3 alone, so it is said "by one account".
- I know de Cogan's analysis (C19, C20) only through S2. Read de Cogan or Hunt (S8) before the reopened verdict is recorded.
- The inquiry's formal name is not in what I read, so the script says "an official inquiry".
- I have not read the 1866 cable's design (bigger core? purer copper?) or its signalling speed. The ending therefore claims no cause for the success, and no speed.
- S3 says "Both 1865 and 1866 cables succeeded", but nothing I read describes the 1865 attempt. Unverified, and not used.
- The mirror galvanometer's appearance (lamp, tiny mirror, light spot on a scale) is not described in what I read. Check it against a museum record before shot S9. Likewise the coil's real shape (S10) before shot S5, and the people's likenesses from period engravings.

## Content rules applied
- Left out: the Trinity Church service in New York's 1858 celebrations (a religious device; the fireworks carry the celebration instead).
- Left out: the "end of the Indian Mutiny" news the cable carried (war news the story does not need).
- For T2: the dogs' fate and the frostbite injuries.
- For T3: the legend's darker tales of ruin.
- Whitehouse is to be told fairly, never mocked: the film reopens his verdict rather than humiliating him.
- No one dies in T1's story. Every person pictured is an adult.
